analysis.one_liner: Gives nannies, home care aides, and housekeepers overtime pay, sick days, written contracts, and basic workplace rights.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 12, 2025 with 115 cosponsors — every one a Democrat — the bill was sent to six House committees and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bring the roughly 2.2 million people who clean homes, care for children, and look after seniors and people with disabilities under basic workplace protections most other workers already have. It would end the federal exemption that denies overtime pay to live-in domestic workers, require written contracts, guarantee paid sick days, meal and rest breaks, and advance notice of schedule changes, extend federal anti-discrimination law to domestic workers, and create a national hotline, a standards board, and enforcement grants. It also temporarily increases federal Medicaid payments to help cover the cost for home care paid through Medicaid. The bill was introduced in June 2025 with 115 cosponsors — all Democrats — and referred to six House committees, where it has sat without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: About 2.2 million domestic workers — roughly 9 in 10 of them women, disproportionately women of color and immigrants — would gain overtime pay for live-in work, paid sick days, written contracts, rest breaks, protection from wage deductions and retaliation, and access to federal anti-discrimination law. Families who depend on in-home care would also benefit from lower turnover and more stable care relationships, which the bill's findings link to better working conditions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nannies, housekeepers, and home care aides

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act exemption that has denied overtime pay to live-in domestic employees, so nannies and home care aides who live with their employers would earn time-and-a-half beyond 40 hours a week.

Guarantees earned paid sick days: one hour for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for the worker's own illness, a family member's care, or situations involving domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Requires a signed written agreement, in a language the worker understands, covering pay, hours, breaks, termination policy, and grievance procedures — and bans forced arbitration clauses, nondisclosure agreements, and noncompetes in those agreements.
Gives live-in workers termination protections: 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance pay, plus guaranteed access to phone and internet so isolated workers can communicate with the outside world.
Extends Title VII of the Civil Rights Act — federal protection against workplace discrimination and harassment — to domestic workers who are currently left out in practice.

Creates a Domestic Employee Standards Board, a federal enforcement task force, a national hotline, and grants for community-based outreach, and makes it illegal to retaliate against a worker by threatening to report her immigration status.
Temporarily raises the federal Medicaid match for services provided by domestic employees to help home care agencies and state programs absorb the new labor standards.

analysis.who_pays: The households and businesses that employ domestic workers — private families, staffing agencies, and Medicaid-funded home care providers — would bear the cost of overtime, sick days, scheduling-notice pay, and written agreements. Federal and state Medicaid programs would absorb a temporary increase in matching payments, and taxpayers fund the hotline, standards board, and outreach grants. Some families might respond by hiring fewer hours or paying more for care.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and care agencies that employ them

drawbacks.text: The cost of overtime, paid sick days, severance for live-in workers, and scheduling-notice pay falls on private households and small home care businesses, not large corporations. Families paying out of pocket for a nanny or an aide for an aging parent would face higher costs, and some might reduce hours or hire informally instead.

The bill raises federal Medicaid spending by temporarily increasing the federal match for services provided by domestic employees (Title IV), adding to federal health program costs, and it directs new spending on a standards board, an enforcement task force, a national hotline, and community outreach grants.

The sick-day provision caps accrual at 56 hours per year and imposes documentation requirements for absences longer than three days, so workers with longer caregiving emergencies would still face gaps, and enforcement depends on workers coming forward in an industry where, by the bill's own findings, 91 percent of those with problems did not complain for fear of losing their job.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted: millions of workers in one of the least-regulated corners of the labor market would gain overtime, paid sick days, contracts, and real anti-retaliation tools, at wages where a few unpaid hours materially matter. The costs are real and fall heavily on private households and small care businesses rather than on large corporations, and higher Medicaid matching funds only partially offset the compliance burden in publicly funded care. The bill is broadly drafted (nearly every household employer is covered) rather than phased in by employer size, which makes compliance harder for families hiring a single aide. It died in committee before any of these tradeoffs were tested in a hearing or amendment process, so there is no record of how the concerns were addressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to six House committees on the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing, no vote, and no movement.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act in the House on June 12, 2025.
On the same day, the bill was referred to six committees: Education and Workforce, House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary.
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral — the bill has not moved since June 12, 2025.
The bill has 115 cosponsors, all of them Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

The bill's own findings cite an estimated 2.2 million domestic employees, an average wage of about $16.79 an hour, and documented patterns of wage theft, uncontracted work, and exclusion from overtime, civil rights, and labor law protections.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: households and agencies that employ domestic workers continue under current rules with no new obligations, while the 2.2 million workers the bill would cover have gained nothing yet. Because Congress is still in session, the outcome is not final.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households and agencies keeping the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 115 cosponsors are Democrats and none is a Republican, and the Republican-controlled House has taken no action on the bill since it was referred to six committees.

industries.industry: Domestic staffing agencies and on-demand care and cleaning platforms
industries.note: They would bear new obligations — written contracts, paid sick days, scheduling-notice pay — and the bill restricts their ability to deduct wages or penalize workers for communicating directly with customers instead of through the platform. But the bill also encourages the use of fiscal intermediaries, which could steer more work through formal agencies rather than informal arrangements.

industries.industry: Medicaid-funded home care providers and fiscal intermediaries
industries.note: The bill regulates how these providers pay their workforce while simultaneously raising the federal Medicaid match for their services, locking in their role as the channel for publicly funded home care. Better-funded, better-paid home care also improves quality for seniors and people with disabilities who rely on it.

industries.industry: Private households employing domestic workers (nannies, housekeepers, aides)
industries.note: Household employers would carry the cost of overtime, paid sick days, written agreements, and severance for live-in workers. These are largely affluent households, though some are middle-class families paying for eldercare or child care out of pocket.

analysis.trajectory: With six committees of referral, no hearings or markups on the record, no Republican cosponsors, and a Republican House majority, the bill is unlikely to reach the floor this Congress. Most bills at this stage expire when the Congress ends in January 2027 and must be reintroduced from scratch. The main openings would be a shift in House control after the 2026 elections or attachment of its provisions to a larger package, neither of which the current record suggests is imminent.
